chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Salma, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Usama ibn Zayd used to intercede regarding matters in which there was no fixed penalty (Hadd). So a person upon whom a fixed penalty had become obligatory was brought to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). Usama interceded for him. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: 'Intercession is not accepted regarding a fixed penalty (Hadd).'

key_terms.أُسَامَةُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ: Usama ibn Zayd, a companion of the Prophet known for his intercession
key_terms.حَدٌّ: Fixed penalty (Hadd), a specific punishment prescribed in Islamic law
key_terms.لَا يُشَفَّعُ فِي حَدٍّ: Intercession is not accepted regarding a fixed penalty

ai.seo_question: Is intercession accepted for fixed penalties (Hudud) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the legal principle that intercession (Shafa'ah) is invalid for fixed divine penalties (Hudud), illustrating the distinction between the Prophet's authority and human advocacy. It narrates an incident where Usama ibn Zayd, renowned for his intercession, attempted to plead for a specific individual, prompting the Prophet (peace be upon him) to declare that Hudud are not subject to intercession. This ruling underscores the divine nature of these penalties, ensuring they are applied strictly according to God's law rather than human influence.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Al Hakam, from Aban Bin Usman, from Salma, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Asama Bin Zayd used to intercede regarding the thing in which there was no Penalty (Hadd) (applicable). So they came to Rasool-Allahsaww with a person upon whom a Penalty (Hadd) was Obligated, so Asama interceded for him. So Rasool-Allahsaww said to him: ‘There is not intercession regarding a Penalty (Hadd)’.
